books.title: Animals, Animals
books.art_why: Real animals shown today are best represented with photographs.

pages.text: There are many kinds of animals. The elk is in the deer family. Male elk have large antlers. Elk can swim well and run very fast.
pages.brief: A male elk with large antlers stands on land; the same elk swims in water and runs very fast. The elk is shown as a member of the deer family.

pages.text: Giraffes have spots with long necks. Giraffes are very tall on their heads. and short horns all over their bodies.
pages.brief: A very tall giraffe has a long neck and a spotted body. Short horns are visible on its head, and spots cover its body. It stands tall, showing its long neck and spotted pattern.

pages.text: Elephants are the largest land animals. Elephants have long trunks. They live in grasslands and forests.
pages.brief: Elephants, the largest land animals, stand outdoors in grasslands and near forests. Each elephant has a long trunk. One large elephant with a long trunk stands in the open grassland, while others are near forest trees.

pages.text: They have thick fur to keep them warm. Snow leopards live on cold mountains.
pages.brief: A snow leopard with thick fur stands on a cold mountain. Its thick fur is visible as it stays on the cold mountain slope. The snow leopard is shown in the cold mountain place where it lives.

pages.text: This camel has a long winter coat. Camels can live for a long time without food or water.
pages.brief: A camel with a long winter coat stands in the open outdoors. Its long winter coat covers its body. The camel stands calmly, showing how it can live for a long time without food or water.

pages.text: Foxes eat small animals, insects, fruits, and eggs. Foxes live in holes in the ground. The fox is in the dog family.
pages.brief: A fox is shown standing outdoors near a hole in the ground. Around the fox are small animals, insects, fruits, and eggs, the foods it eats. The fox lives in the hole in the ground.

pages.text: The zebra is in the horse family. Zebras have white and black stripes and live in grasslands. The hair on their necks stands straight up.
pages.brief: A zebra with white and black stripes stands in open grassland. The hair on its neck stands straight up. This zebra, a member of the horse family, is shown in the grassland place where it lives.

pages.text: Kangaroos eat grass and other plants. It uses its strong back legs to hop. The great gray kangaroo has a pouch.
pages.brief: A great gray kangaroo with a pouch is shown standing on the ground among grass and other plants outdoors. It uses its strong back legs to hop. The kangaroo eats grass and other plants nearby.

pages.text: The hippopotamus spends most of its time in water. A hippopotamus has almost no hair. It eats grass and water plants.
pages.brief: A hippopotamus with almost no hair is shown in the water. Its body has almost no hair. It spends most of its time in the water. Nearby, the same hippopotamus eats grass and water plants.

pages.text: There are many kinds of animals. They eat seals, birds, and fish. They have thick fur to stay warm. Polar bears live in cold places.
pages.brief: A polar bear with thick fur is shown standing in a cold place. Seals, birds, and fish are nearby. The polar bear has thick fur to stay warm, and it lives in a cold place.

books.title: Weird Bird Beaks
books.art_why: Real birds and their beaks can be photographed.

pages.text: I have feathers on my beak that look like hair. I am a bearded barbet. Bearded Barbet.
pages.brief: A bearded barbet is shown close up, with fine feathers on its beak that look like hair. The bird faces forward so the beak feathers are clearly visible. The focus is on the bird’s head and beak.

pages.text: Crossbill I am a crossbill. My beak is crossed like an X. My beak gets the seeds out of tree cones.
pages.brief: A crossbill is at a tree cone, its beak crossed like an X. The bird uses the crossed beak to get seeds out of the cone. The tree cone and the crossed beak are the main focus.

pages.text: I use it to knock down fruit. I have a horn on top of my beak. I am a rhinoceros hornbill. Rhinoceros Hornbill.
pages.brief: A rhinoceros hornbill is shown with a horn on top of its beak. The bird uses its beak to knock down fruit. The horn and the beak are clearly visible as the bird reaches toward the fruit.

pages.text: Sword-Billed Hummingbird I am a sword-billed hummingbird. I use my long beak to drink from flowers.
pages.brief: A sword-billed hummingbird is at a flower with its very long beak. The bird uses the long beak to drink from the flower. The flower and the hummingbird’s long beak are the main focus of the scene.

pages.text: I can hold fish in the skin under my beak. I am a brown pelican. Brown Pelican.
pages.brief: A brown pelican is shown with fish held in the skin under its beak. The pouch beneath the beak stretches to hold the fish. The pelican’s beak and the fish in the pouch are the main focus.

pages.text: Shoebill Stork I am a shoebill stork. My beak is shaped like a shoe.
pages.brief: A shoebill stork is shown close up so its beak is clearly visible. The beak has a shape like a shoe. The focus is on the bird and its unusual beak.

pages.text: My long beak looks like a spoon. I am a spoonbill. Spoonbill.
pages.brief: A spoonbill is shown with its long beak that looks like a spoon. The bird’s head and the spoon-shaped beak are clearly visible. The focus is on the long beak and the bird in a close view.

pages.text: Toucan I am a toucan. My huge and colorful beak is very light.
pages.brief: A toucan is shown with its huge, colorful beak. The beak looks very light. The bird holds its head steady so the large colorful beak is easy to see.

pages.text: Which beak is your favorite? Many birds have weird beaks.
pages.brief: Several different birds with unusual beaks are shown together. Each bird has a different weird beak shape, so the group shows many kinds of beaks. The birds fill the scene with their strange beaks, inviting a choice of favorite.

books.title: Summer Olympic Events
books.art_why: Modern Olympic events are real and can be photographed.

pages.text: The Summer Olympic Games The Summer Olympics are held every four years. They are held in cities around the world.
pages.brief: A wide view of a large Olympic stadium in a city, filled with athletes and crowds. People gather to watch the Summer Olympic Games take place in the city. The scene shows the Games being held in a city, with athletes and spectators together.

pages.text: Let’s look at some of the games.
pages.brief: Several Olympic athletes are shown taking part in different events at a summer venue. They stand or move in separate parts of the scene, giving a look at some of the games. The picture presents a variety of Summer Olympic Games.

pages.text: Water Sports There are many water sports. One water sport is swimming.
pages.brief: Swimmers race through a bright blue swimming pool during a water sport event. Several athletes swim in the water, with splashes around their arms and legs. The scene focuses on swimming as one of the water sports at the Summer Olympics.

pages.text: Some swimming races use only one kind of stroke. Other races use many strokes.
pages.brief: A swimming pool shows swimmers using different strokes in separate races. In one part, a swimmer uses a single stroke along the water. In another part, swimmers use several strokes as they race. The scene shows both kinds of swimming races.

pages.text: Another water sport is diving. Divers jump from high above the water.
pages.brief: A diver stands high on a diving platform above a swimming pool, preparing to jump. Another diver is already in the air, falling toward the water below. The scene shows diving, a water sport where divers jump from high above the water.

pages.text: Track and Field Track and field events are games of running, throwing, and jumping. Races can be short or long.
pages.brief: Runners race on a track while other athletes take part in throwing and jumping events on the field. Some runners sprint in a short race, and others run a longer distance. The scene shows track and field games of running, throwing, and jumping.

pages.text: In throwing games, people win by throwing objects the farthest.
pages.brief: An athlete in a throwing event stands in an open field and throws an object as far as possible. The object travels through the air across the field. The scene shows how people win throwing games by throwing objects the farthest.

pages.text: In the high jump, people leap over a bar. In the long jump, people leap as far as they can.
pages.brief: One athlete leaps high over a bar in the high jump, clearing it with a strong jump. Nearby, another athlete leaps forward as far as possible in the long jump. The scene shows both jumping events, with athletes leaping over a bar and leaping for distance.

pages.text: Gymnastics Gymnasts leap, flip, and twirl. They need strength, skill, and good timing.
pages.brief: Gymnasts leap, flip, and twirl in a bright gymnastics hall. One gymnast is in midair during a flip, while another twists through a turn. The scene shows gymnasts using strength, skill, and good timing as they move.

pages.text: Gymnasts compete on the balance beam. They must balance on the beam while they turn and flip.
pages.brief: A gymnast balances on a balance beam in a gymnastics competition. The gymnast turns and flips while keeping steady on the beam. The scene shows the strength and skill needed to balance on the beam while turning and flipping.

pages.text: Gymnasts compete on the rings. They hold onto the rings and flip their bodies in circles.
pages.brief: A gymnast holds onto the rings and flips their body in circles during a gymnastics competition. The athlete hangs from the rings with strong arms, moving in a circular motion. The scene shows a gymnast competing on the rings at the Summer Olympics.

pages.text: The Summer Olympics include many sports. Which sports do you like? Summer Olympic Sports.
pages.brief: A group of Olympic athletes from different sports stand together in a stadium. Swimmers, runners, and gymnasts are shown side by side, representing the many sports in the Summer Olympics. The scene invites viewers to think about which sports they like.

books.title: Legs, Wings, Fins, and Flippers
books.art_why: Real animals that exist today are shown moving in familiar habitats.

pages.text: Introduction Animals move in many ways. Animals have different body parts to help them move.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor scene showing several different animals moving at once: a horse trotting across grass, a bird flying overhead, a fish swimming in a pond, and a frog mid-leap. Each animal is clearly visible with its legs, wings or fins doing the work of moving.

pages.text: On Land Most animals that live on land have legs. Animals can have different numbers of legs.
pages.brief: A grassy land scene with animals standing and walking on their legs. A horse on long legs stands beside a small group of insects with many tiny legs, and a frog crouches nearby, showing that land animals have legs in very different numbers.

pages.text: Horses have long legs to run fast. Frogs have long back legs to leap.
pages.brief: Two panels of action on open ground: a horse with long legs galloping fast across a field, and a frog with long back legs pushing off to leap into the air above a pond edge, both bodies stretched in motion.

pages.text: Some animals have no legs. These animals slide their bodies to move.
pages.brief: Close view of a snake sliding its long body across dry ground, and beside it an earthworm pushing through soft soil. Neither animal has legs, and both bodies are bent in curves as they move forward.

pages.text: Do You Know? In the Air Birds, bats, and many insects use wings to fly. Animals can have two wings or four wings.
pages.brief: Open sky above trees and flowers, filled with flying animals: a bird with outstretched wings, a bat with leathery wings, and insects such as a butterfly and a dragonfly, showing wings of different shapes and numbers in the air.

pages.text: Chicks can’t fly until they grow strong feathers.
pages.brief: A nest on a branch holding a small fluffy chick with tiny stubby wings, flapping them while an adult bird perches nearby. The chick stays in the nest, its feathers short and soft, not yet strong enough for flight.

pages.text: Animal wings come in many shapes and sizes.
pages.brief: A clear comparison view of several animal wings arranged in the open: a large bird wing, a wide butterfly wing, a small bee wing and a bat wing, all different shapes and sizes, resting against a plain natural background.

pages.text: In Water Fish use fins and tails to move through the water.
pages.brief: Underwater scene in clear blue water: a fish swimming forward with its fins spread and its tail curved, pushing through the water past green water plants and smooth stones on the sandy bottom.

pages.text: Whales have fins and flippers. But seals, sea lions, and sea turtles only have flippers.
pages.brief: Ocean scene showing a whale gliding with fins and flippers, and nearby a seal, a sea lion and a sea turtle swimming, each with flippers only. The water is blue and the animals are clearly in motion.

pages.text: Penguins are birds, but they have flippers instead of wings. Penguins swim to hunt fish in the ocean. On land, they can walk, or they can slide on their bellies.
pages.brief: A penguin swimming fast underwater with flippers spread wide, chasing small fish. Beside it, another penguin on icy land walks upright, and a third slides along on its belly across the cold ground.

pages.text: Some animals that live in water have webbed feet. Webbed feet help animals swim better.
pages.brief: Close view of webbed feet on an animal standing at the edge of a pond, the skin stretched between the toes. The animal pushes into the water, the wide webbed feet spread out to help it swim.

pages.text: Conclusion Watch how animals move in the world around you. Think about the body parts that help animals move. Think about how you move, too!
pages.brief: A lively outdoor scene of animals moving all around: a bird flying, a horse running, a fish in water and a frog leaping, with a child watching from the side, looking closely at the legs, wings and fins in action.

books.title: Goats Are Great!
books.art_why: Real goats exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: What’s so great about goats? Goats give us food. They help us and play with us. Goats make great pets.
pages.brief: A sunny farmyard with several friendly goats near a child. One goat stands by a pile of food, another walks close to the child, and a third rests as a pet. The goats look helpful and playful, showing how they can give food, help people, and be good pets.

pages.text: Goats provide food for us. Many people drink goat milk. Goat milk makes goat cheese! Some people eat goat meat.
pages.brief: A bright table with a glass of goat milk, a round of goat cheese, and a cooked goat-meat dish. Two people sit nearby, one drinking the milk and another reaching for the cheese. The display shows the foods that goats provide for people.

pages.text: Goats help us in many ways. Goats are happy to eat weeds in people’s yards. We can make wool cloth out of soft goat hair.
pages.brief: A tidy backyard garden where goats nibble weeds among plants. A person nearby gathers soft goat hair in their hands. Beside them, a folded piece of wool cloth shows what can be made from the hair. The goats are busy helping clear the yard.

pages.text: Goats make great pets and are fun to play with. Goats learn to come when you call their name. Goats are easy to take care of.
pages.brief: A grassy yard where a child calls to a goat by name. The goat walks toward the child, looking responsive and friendly. Another goat stands nearby as an easy pet to care for. The scene shows goats learning to come when called and being fun to play with.

pages.text: Goats like to be outdoors. They enjoy sunny days. Goats spend most of their day playing and eating.
pages.brief: A sunny outdoor meadow with several goats spending the day outside. Some goats play together while others graze and rest on the grass. Bright sunlight fills the scene, showing goats enjoying a sunny day outdoors and filling most of their time playing and eating.

pages.text: Goats are great to look at. Many have long, floppy ears. Goats have only lower teeth. All goats have two hard toes on each foot.
pages.brief: A close view of several goats in a sunny field. One goat has long, floppy ears. Another shows its lower teeth while eating. A third goat stands so its foot and two hard toes are clearly visible, showing features people can look at.

pages.text: Both boy and girl goats can have long beards. Some baby goats are born with tiny horns. Goat hair is very soft to touch.
pages.brief: A gentle close-up of goats with long beards. A boy goat and a girl goat both have beards. A baby goat stands nearby with tiny horns. A person’s hand gently touches the soft goat hair, showing how soft it feels.

pages.text: Goats eat healthy foods. Goats like to eat long grass. They like flowers and apples. Goats eat anything yummy.
pages.brief: A green pasture with goats eating healthy foods. One goat stretches up to nibble long grass. Another sniffs bright flowers, and a third leans toward a red apple on the ground. The goats look happy as they eat the yummy foods around them.

pages.text: Goats are strong and quick. Goats like to climb and jump. They play king of the mountain!
pages.brief: A rocky hillside where goats climb and jump. One goat leaps from rock to rock while another stands tall on a high ledge. Two goats face each other as if playing king of the mountain. The scene shows how strong and quick goats can be.

pages.text: Goats are smart, playful, gentle, and helpful. Goats are fun and friendly. That’s why goats are great!
pages.brief: A cheerful farmyard gathering of smart, playful, gentle, and helpful goats. Some goats play together, one stands calmly beside a child, and another follows a person. The friendly goats fill the sunny scene, showing why goats are fun, friendly, and great.

books.title: At a Touch Tank
books.art_why: Real coastal touch-tank animals can be photographed today.

pages.text: This touch tank has animals from the coast of Alaska. They live in very cold water.
pages.brief: A touch tank holds several animals from the coast of Alaska. The animals live in very cold water inside the tank. The tank shows a cold coastal habitat with room for the creatures to stay in the water.

pages.text: Sea stars live in this touch tank.
pages.brief: Several sea stars live inside the touch tank. Their arms spread out across the tank surface. The sea stars rest in the water among the other coastal animals in the tank. The water covers them.

pages.text: This blood star is red like blood. It has five arms, like most sea stars. It feels rough when I touch it. Blood stars eat sponges and tiny ocean animals.
pages.brief: A red blood star rests in the touch tank. It has five arms spread out from its center. A child's fingers touch the rough surface of the star. Nearby are sponges and tiny ocean animals that blood stars eat.

pages.text: Anemones live in this touch tank.
pages.brief: Several anemones are inside the touch tank. The touch tank holds the anemones in water. The anemones live there, and the tank is full of water for them. The anemones sit together in the tank.

pages.text: This anemone is pale pink. It has many soft tentacles. The tentacles gently grab my fingers when I touch them. Anemones eat little shrimp and fish.
pages.brief: A pale pink anemone sits in the touch tank. It has many soft tentacles spread around it. A child's fingers touch the tentacles, and the tentacles gently grab the fingers. Little shrimp and fish are nearby in the water.

pages.text: Sea urchins live in this touch tank.
pages.brief: Several sea urchins live in the touch tank. The sea urchins are inside the tank in the water. They live there with the water around them, and the tank holds the sea urchins in one place.

pages.text: This red sea urchin has many long spines. The sharp spines move when I touch them. Red sea urchins eat seaweed and other ocean plants.
pages.brief: A red sea urchin sits in the touch tank. It has many long, sharp spines sticking out from its body. A child's fingers touch the spines, and the sharp spines move. Seaweed and other ocean plants are nearby in the water.

pages.text: Sea cucumbers live in this touch tank.
pages.brief: Several sea cucumbers live in the touch tank. The sea cucumbers are inside the tank in the water. They live there, and the tank holds the sea cucumbers with water around them. The sea cucumbers rest in the tank.

pages.text: This sea cucumber is the color of a brick. Its body is covered with little bumps. The bumps look sharp, but they feel soft. Sea cucumbers eat tiny plants and animals in the ocean.
pages.brief: A brick-colored sea cucumber sits in the touch tank. Its body is covered with little bumps. The bumps look sharp, but a child's fingers touch them and they feel soft. Tiny plants and animals are nearby in the water.

pages.text: I never poke, pull, squeeze, or move the animals. I touch all of them gently with just two fingers. I want all the animals to stay safe.
pages.brief: A child's hand reaches into the touch tank with only two fingers extended. The two fingers touch an animal very gently. The child does not poke, pull, squeeze, or move the animals. The animals stay safe in the water.

books.title: What Lives in This Hole?
books.art_why: Real animals, burrows, and a child's school research are shown in the present-day world.

pages.text: Animal Burrows Many animals live in holes called burrows. I wanted to know more about them.
pages.brief: A curious child stands at the edge of a small patch of ground with several dark burrow openings, looking at the holes and wanting to learn more about the many animals that live inside them.

pages.text: My teacher helped me learn about them. I used the computer to share what I learned. Come see what I learned!
pages.brief: A teacher sits beside a child at a computer, pointing to the screen as the child prepares to share what they learned about burrows; the child looks eagerly ready to show the information to others.

pages.text: Staying Cool A tortoise lives in this hole! It lives in a desert. It digs a burrow to get away from the heat.
pages.brief: A tortoise digs a burrow in dry desert ground, its shell dusty and its legs working at the soil; the deep hole gives the animal a cool place to escape the heat of the hot sun.

pages.text: Wowser! Keeping Eggs Safe A big spider lives in this hole! It lays eggs in a little bag. It takes the bag when it leaves to find food.
pages.brief: A big spider rests at the entrance of its underground hole, a small egg bag held close near the soil; the spider carries the bag with it as it leaves the burrow to search for food.

pages.text: Making a Nest This is a hole for puffins! They spend most of their time at sea.
pages.brief: A puffin floats on the sea near a rocky cliff, spending most of its time on the water; a burrow hole in the cliff soil shows where this sea bird makes its home when it comes to land.

pages.text: Wowser! They dig a burrow on a cliff. The burrow is a nest. Both parents take care of the egg.
pages.brief: Two puffins stand at a burrow dug into a windy cliff, the hole serving as their nest; both parent birds stay close to the single egg, taking care of it together on the rocky ledge.

pages.text: Living in the Dark Naked mole rats live in this hole! They live in the dark.
pages.brief: Several naked mole rats cluster inside a deep, dark underground hole, their wrinkled pink bodies pressed together in the dim tunnel; this burrow is where they live together in the dark, away from any light.

pages.text: They dig tunnels to find food. One animal digs. Others move the dirt away.
pages.brief: Inside the dark underground burrow, one naked mole rat digs at the soil with its feet to make a tunnel for finding food, while other naked mole rats push the loose dirt away behind it, working together.

pages.text: Hiding and Laying Eggs A big salamander lives in this underwater hole! It lives in rivers and streams. It hides all day and hunts at night.
pages.brief: A big salamander rests quietly inside an underwater hole in a river or stream, hiding in the dim water during the day; its long body stays tucked in the burrow until it hunts at night.

pages.text: The burrow is a safe place for eggs. A female lays many eggs. A male keeps the eggs safe.
pages.brief: Inside an underwater burrow, a female salamander has laid a cluster of many eggs; a male salamander stays close beside the eggs, guarding the safe nest in the clear water of the river or stream.

pages.text: Wowser! Taking a Nap A wombat lives in this hole! It sleeps in its burrow all day. It comes out to find food at night.
pages.brief: A wombat sleeps curled up inside its earthen burrow through the quiet day; later, under the night sky above, the same wombat slowly comes out of the hole to search for food in the dark.

pages.text: More to Come Other animals live in burrows, too. It is so fun to learn about animals!
pages.brief: A happy child smiles beside a patch of ground with several burrow openings, with more animals hidden in holes nearby; the scene suggests there are still more burrow animals to learn about and enjoy discovering.

books.title: Pocket Parks
books.art_why: Pocket parks, city lots, workers, statues and ponds are real places and things that can be photographed today.

pages.text: What Is a Pocket Park? Some cities don’t have space for big, grassy parks. That’s why they build pocket parks instead.
pages.brief: A busy city street lined with tall buildings, with one small pocket park tucked between them. The small green space sits where a big grassy park would not fit, showing how cities build pocket parks in crowded places.

pages.text: A pocket park is like a regular park, only smaller. A pocket park can take up a city block. It can also be as small as a parking space.
pages.brief: One pocket park takes up a whole city block in a busy city. Nearby, another pocket park is as small as a single parking space. The two views show the very different sizes a pocket park can have.

pages.text: Lots of Empty Lots An empty lot is a great place for a pocket park. It can take many workers to build one.
pages.brief: An empty lot with bare ground sits between city buildings. Several workers use tools and equipment to turn the empty lot into a pocket park. The workers show how building a pocket park can take many people.

pages.text: People who live close by can help, too. They can plant flowers or trees. They can also help keep the park clean and safe. Every pocket park is different.
pages.brief: People who live close to a pocket park help inside it. Some plant flowers or small trees, while others clean the park and help keep it safe. Their different work shows that every pocket park is different and that nearby neighbors can help.

pages.text: Different Pocket Parks This pocket park has a waterfall at the back. It also has many places for people to sit.
pages.brief: A pocket park with a waterfall at the back and many places for people to sit. The waterfall stands behind the seating area, and several people sit quietly together nearby in the pocket park, facing it.

pages.text: Check out the colorful art at this pocket park. It has a swing to play on, too.
pages.brief: A pocket park showing colorful art across its surfaces. A swing hangs there for play. In this view, the bright colors and the swing make the small park a very cheerful, playful and inviting place.

pages.text: People decorated this pocket park with many lights. They twinkle at night.
pages.brief: A pocket park at night, decorated with many lights. Small lights twinkle across the park and glow against the darkness. The small lit park looks very warm and inviting in the quiet, peaceful night scene.

pages.text: An artist made a statue for this pocket park. It reminds people of someone important.
pages.brief: A pocket park with a statue made by an artist. The statue stands in the park and reminds people of someone important. Nearby, people pause quietly and look at the statue with respect.

pages.text: This pocket park has grass and a large pond. People can come here to think.
pages.brief: A pocket park with green grass and a large pond. A person sits beside the pond in the quiet park, thinking. The grass and water make a calm place where people can come to think.

pages.text: A man paints a big snake and turtle in this pocket park. They look as if they would be fun to play on.
pages.brief: A man paints a big snake and turtle in a pocket park. He works on the painted creatures, which look as if they would be fun to play on. The large snake and turtle fill part of the small park with color.

pages.text: This tiny pocket park is almost hidden in trees. People can relax and listen to the waterfall.
pages.brief: A tiny pocket park almost hidden among trees. A small waterfall flows in the park, and people relax nearby, listening to the water. The trees surround the little park and make it feel quiet and tucked away.

pages.text: Conclusion Pocket parks can be found all over. Do you have a pocket park where you live?
pages.brief: Pocket parks can be found all over, in many parts of a city. Several small pocket parks appear near homes and streets, showing that these tiny green places exist in many neighborhoods. The scene suggests looking for a pocket park close to where people live.

books.title: The Butterfly Life Cycle
books.art_why: Monarch butterflies exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: The Life Cycle A monarch butterfly has four stages in its life cycle.
pages.brief: A monarch butterfly is shown with its wings spread open, representing the four stages of its life cycle. This is the first view of the butterfly whose life cycle will be shown from start to finish.

pages.text: Egg A female monarch butterfly lays an egg on a leaf. A caterpillar grows inside the tiny egg. The egg hatches in three to twelve days.
pages.brief: A female monarch butterfly stands on a leaf and lays a tiny egg on its surface. A close view shows the tiny egg with a small caterpillar growing inside it. The egg will hatch in three to twelve days.

pages.text: The hungry caterpillar eats all the time. First, the caterpillar eats its own eggshell. Then, the caterpillar eats the leaf it is on.
pages.brief: A hungry caterpillar sits on a leaf and eats. First it chews its own empty eggshell beside it. Then it turns and eats the leaf it is on, eating all the time. The caterpillar keeps eating without stopping.

pages.text: The caterpillar grows quickly. Its skin does not grow. The caterpillar’s skin splits and peels away.
pages.brief: A caterpillar has grown quickly and is now large. Its old skin splits along its body and peels away. The old skin slips off because the caterpillar's skin does not grow as the caterpillar grows.

pages.text: Do You Know? New skin is under the old skin. The caterpillar sheds its skin four to six times. The caterpillar grows for two to four weeks.
pages.brief: A caterpillar is shown with new skin revealed under the old skin peeling away. The caterpillar sheds its skin four to six times. It grows for two to four weeks, becoming larger each time it sheds.

pages.text: Pupa When the caterpillar is grown, it hangs from a branch. It sheds its skin one last time. The new skin is bright green.
pages.brief: A grown caterpillar hangs upside down from a branch. It sheds its skin one last time. The new skin underneath is bright green. The caterpillar hangs from the branch as the old skin falls away.

pages.text: This green skin becomes hard. The caterpillar is now a pupa. It will stay inside its shell for one to two weeks.
pages.brief: The bright green skin becomes hard. The caterpillar is now a pupa. The pupa hangs from the branch inside its hard shell. It will stay inside this shell for one to two weeks, waiting.

pages.text: Adult Butterfly The pupa comes out of its shell. It is now a butterfly. Its wings are wet.
pages.brief: The pupa comes out of its shell. It is now an adult butterfly. Its wings are wet as it emerges from the shell. The new butterfly is shown with its wet wings for the first time.

pages.text: The new butterfly rests. The butterfly must hang upside down, or it will not be able to fly.
pages.brief: A new butterfly rests, hanging upside down from a branch. It must hang upside down. If it does not hang upside down, it will not be able to fly. The butterfly stays still in this position.

pages.text: The butterfly hangs for three to four hours. The sun and air dry its wings.
pages.brief: The butterfly hangs upside down for three to four hours. The sun and the air dry its wings. In the open air, the butterfly waits while sunlight and moving air reach its wet wings and dry them.

pages.text: Then, the butterfly is able to fly. It flies off to eat. It also searches for a mate.
pages.brief: The butterfly is now able to fly. It flies off to eat, and it also searches for a mate. It is ready to fly. The butterfly flies away into the air, looking for food and a mate.

pages.text: A monarch butterfly may only live for two to six weeks. The female monarch lays her eggs. The butterfly life cycle starts again.
pages.brief: An adult monarch butterfly may live only two to six weeks. A female monarch lays her eggs. The butterfly life cycle starts again. The female monarch is shown laying eggs as the cycle begins once more.

books.title: Elephants: Giant Mammals
books.art_why: Elephants are real animals that exist today and are photographed in nature.

pages.text: Elephants are Number One! Elephants are huge! They are much, much bigger than the biggest human. They are the biggest land animals on Earth.
pages.brief: A huge elephant stands on a grassy savanna, its body towering over a nearby adult human. The elephant’s tall legs and massive head show it is much bigger than the person. Open sky and low grass fill the background.

pages.text: Take a Look Elephants are covered with thick gray or brown skin. They have long noses called trunks.
pages.brief: A close view of an elephant’s wrinkled gray skin and long trunk curling down from its face. The thick hide covers its large body. The trunk hangs forward, showing its length. Warm sunlight falls on the elephant’s head and back.

pages.text: Elephants use their trunks to breathe and make noise. They also use their trunks to grab food and suck up water.
pages.brief: An elephant raises its trunk high and opens its mouth to trumpet. Its trunk then curls around a leafy branch, and the tip dips into a small pool of water. The elephant stands on open grassland.

pages.text: Two Kinds of Elephants There are African and Asian elephants. African elephants are bigger than Asian elephants. The two kinds are different in other ways, too.
pages.brief: Two elephants stand side by side on a grassy plain. The African elephant on the left is clearly larger than the Asian elephant on the right. Both stand facing forward, their trunks hanging down and their thick skin visible.

pages.text: Growing up... and up Baby elephants weigh more than most adult humans. The mother teaches her calf how to live in the wild.
pages.brief: A baby elephant stands on a grassy plain beside an adult human. The calf is young but solid and heavy. The mother elephant stands close behind, her trunk touching the calf’s back. The calf looks toward the mother.

pages.text: Elephants live in groups like a family. Adult elephants in the group help keep the young ones safe.
pages.brief: A family group of elephants stands together on an open savanna. Several adult elephants surround the smaller young ones, their large bodies forming a protective circle. The young elephants stay close to the adults. Dry grass and scattered trees fill the background.

pages.text: Don’t Eat Me! Huge elephants don’t have to worry about other animals. Lions and tigers know adult elephants are too big to attack.
pages.brief: A huge adult elephant stands on a grassy plain. A lion and a tiger watch from a distance, keeping low in the grass. The elephant’s large body and strong legs show it is too big for them to attack. The predators stay back.

pages.text: Time to Leave After ten to fifteen years, young males leave their groups. They go to live alone or with other males. Female elephants stay together in their own group.
pages.brief: A young male elephant walks away from a family group across a grassy plain. Behind him, adult females and young elephants stay together in a group. Another male elephant stands alone in the distance. The sky is wide and open.

pages.text: Plenty of Plants Elephants eat a lot of grass and leaves in one day. It takes an adult human one hundred days to eat as much.
pages.brief: An adult elephant stands among tall grass and leafy bushes, its trunk pulling a large bundle of plants toward its mouth. A small pile of food sits beside an adult human in the background. The elephant’s pile is much larger. Green plants spread across the scene.

pages.text: Asian and African Giants Elephants are smart animals that take good care of each other. They are very special animals.
pages.brief: Two elephants stand close together on a grassy plain. One elephant’s trunk rests gently near the other’s head, as if caring for it. Their large bodies and calm faces show they are intelligent animals. The open savanna stretches behind them.

books.title: Condors: Giant Birds
books.art_why: Condors are real animals that exist today.

pages.text: A Very Big Bird Condors are huge birds. wing One can be almost as long as a bicycle.
pages.brief: A huge condor stands in an open outdoor space with its wing stretched out wide. Its long wing reaches nearly the length of a bicycle shown beside it, making the bird’s great size easy to see.

pages.text: Condor Homes These big birds like wide-open spaces. They need lots of room to land.
pages.brief: Several condors gather in a wide-open landscape with plenty of clear space around them. One condor comes down to land on the open ground, while the others stand nearby. Their wide wings need space.

pages.text: Condors fly high to look for food. They can fly for a long time.
pages.brief: High in the sky, a condor flies with its broad wings spread. It looks down over the land below, searching for food, and keeps gliding for a long time. The big bird stays up in the sky as it travels.

pages.text: Condors live in high places. They dry their wings in the sun after bathing. They make nests on rocky cliffs and in trees.
pages.brief: In a high rocky place, condors rest in the sun after bathing. One spreads its wings to dry, while others perch near nests built on rocky cliffs and in trees around them. The high ground is their home.

pages.text: Time to Clean Up Condors can eat all kinds of dead animals. They may eat a small rabbit or a big whale.
pages.brief: A condor stands beside dead animals in an open area. It may eat a small rabbit, and a huge dead whale lies nearby, showing that condors can clean up many kinds of dead animals. The bird feeds on what it finds.

pages.text: Condors can eat dead animals without getting sick.
pages.brief: A condor feeds on a dead animal on the ground. The bird looks healthy and unharmed as it eats, showing that condors can eat dead animals without getting sick. The condor continues eating calmly and shows no sign of illness.

pages.text: From the Neck Up Some condors have white feathers around their necks. Others are all black. Condors do not have feathers on their heads.
pages.brief: Two condors stand side by side. One has white feathers around its neck, while the other is all black. Both have bare heads with no feathers on top. Their necks and heads are clearly visible.

pages.text: Condor heads can change colors. The color shows how the condors are feeling.
pages.brief: A close view of a condor’s head shows its bare skin changing color. The color on its head shifts as the bird shows how it is feeling. No feathers cover the head, so the color is easy to see.

pages.text: Condors Grow Up Mother condors lay one egg every two years. Both parents take care of the egg. The baby condor comes out of the egg after two months. Six months later, it starts to fly. Condors can live almost as long as a person.
pages.brief: At a nest on a high cliff, mother and father condors care for one egg. A baby condor comes out of the egg after two months, and a young condor later starts to fly. An older condor rests nearby; condors can live almost as long as a person.

pages.text: There are very few condors today. People watch condors to keep them safe.
pages.brief: Only a few condors are shown in a wide landscape. People stand at a distance and watch the condors, staying nearby to keep the rare birds safe. There are very few condors left today. The people keep watch.

pages.text: Big Wings in the Sky Condors are special birds. They are some of the largest flying birds in the world.
pages.brief: A condor soars high in the sky with its big wings spread wide. It is one of the largest flying birds in the world, and it looks special as it glides above the land. The bird is impressive.

books.title: Blue Whales: Giant Mammals
books.art_why: Blue whales are real animals alive today, so real photographs exist.

pages.text: A Whale of an Animal The blue whale is the biggest animal on Earth. It is longer than three school buses. It is as heavy as thirty-three elephants!
pages.brief: A blue whale swims through open blue ocean, its long body stretching across the scene. Beside it, three yellow school buses line up end to end to show its length, and a row of thirty-three elephants stands together to show its weight. Bright daylight, calm sea.

pages.text: All mammals Look Out for the Spout A blue whale has two holes on top of its head. The whale uses the holes to breathe.
pages.brief: Close view of the top of a blue whale's head at the ocean surface. Two blowholes sit on top of the head, open and clear. The whale's broad grey back and the water around it fill the picture, with sunlight shining on the waves.

pages.text: The blue whale swims to the surface of the ocean. Water and air shoot up from the holes!
pages.brief: The blue whale floats at the surface of the ocean. A tall spout of water and air shoots up from the two holes on its head, spraying high above it. Ripples spread across the water and the sky is wide and bright behind.

pages.text: Listen for the Song Blue whales sing as they swim. Whale songs are low and loud. The song can be heard far away.
pages.brief: A blue whale swims steadily through deep blue water, singing as it goes. The low, loud song spreads out far through the ocean beyond the whale, shown as gentle waves of sound in the water. Soft light filters down from the surface.

pages.text: Filling Up on Small Stuff Blue whales eat tiny animals and plants. Blue whales dive to find food.
pages.brief: A blue whale dives down through the ocean, its huge body angled toward the depths. All around it drift clouds of tiny animals and plants, the food it has come down to find. The water darkens with depth as the whale descends.

pages.text: A whale opens its mouth. Tiny animals and plants flow in with the water.
pages.brief: The blue whale's enormous mouth opens wide underwater. A thick stream of tiny animals and plants flows in with the seawater, pouring into the great open mouth. The whale's throat stretches and the small creatures swirl around its head.

pages.text: A blue whale has baleen in its mouth. Baleen is like stiff hair.
pages.brief: Close view inside the blue whale's open mouth, showing rows of baleen hanging from the upper jaw. The baleen looks like stiff, bristly hair, packed in long fringes. Water and tiny food drift past the plates, with the huge tongue behind.

pages.text: The water goes out through the baleen. The food stays inside.
pages.brief: Inside the blue whale's mouth, seawater drains out between the fringed baleen plates while the tiny animals and plants stay trapped inside. The baleen hangs in stiff hairy curtains holding the food, and the water streams away through the gaps.

pages.text: Blue whales eat a lot. The food helps them grow blubber. Blubber is a kind of fat. It keeps the whales warm in cold water.
pages.brief: A blue whale swims through cold, grey-green ocean water. A thick layer of blubber shows beneath its skin, the fat that keeps it warm. The whale's rounded body is plump and smooth, and cold water surrounds it on every side.

pages.text: Great Big Babies A baby blue whale is a calf. A calf drinks a lot of milk each day. It grows larger every hour.
pages.brief: A blue whale mother swims beside her small calf in warm blue water. The calf nuzzles close to drink milk, looking round and healthy as it grows larger. The mother's huge body curves around the little one in the open sea.

pages.text: A blue whale mother has one calf at a time. The calf stays with her for a year. Then it swims off to live on its own.
pages.brief: A blue whale mother swims with her one calf close at her side in the open ocean. The calf stays near her, small against her enormous body. Around them the blue water stretches wide, and the pair move slowly along together.

pages.text: The Biggest Animals Blue whales are huge mammals. They are the biggest animals on Earth.
pages.brief: Two enormous blue whales glide through the open ocean, their long bodies filling the scene. Sunlight falls on the water around them, and the whales look vast against the wide blue sea, the biggest animals on Earth.

books.title: The Mighty Mississippi
books.art_why: The book shows real rivers, boats, cities, and animals that exist today.

pages.text: A Long Journey Rain falls. It mixes into the clear waters of a lake.
pages.brief: Rain falls onto a calm, clear lake. The water surface is smooth and transparent, and raindrops mix into it. No river yet, just the lake under a cloudy sky. The rain and lake water blend together.

pages.text: The lake flows into a river. A child could wade across here. This is where the mighty Mississippi River begins.
pages.brief: The lake flows into a narrow, shallow river. The water is clear and calm, low enough that a child could wade across. This small stream is the beginning of the mighty Mississippi River. The river starts here as a small, gentle flow.

pages.text: The water will travel through ten of the fifty United States. It will take three months to reach the sea.
pages.brief: The river winds a long way across the land, passing through ten of the fifty United States. The water moves steadily onward through fields and countryside. It takes three months for the water to travel all the way to the sea.

pages.text: The Upper River At first, the river flows through many locks and dams. They raise or lower the water around the boats. This makes it safe for boats to travel. They also hold back water so boats don’t hit the river bottom.
pages.brief: A boat sits inside a river lock beside a dam. The lock raises or lowers the water around the boat so it can travel safely. The dam holds back water to keep boats from hitting the river bottom.

pages.text: Boats on this part of the river carry wheat and corn down south. The grain helps feed the world.
pages.brief: A line of boats moves down the river carrying wheat and corn. The grain is piled on the boats, heading south. The boats travel on the river under an open sky. This grain helps feed people around the world.

pages.text: A big, dirty river comes in from the west. It mixes with the clear waters of the Mississippi. The Mississippi grows wide and brown.
pages.brief: A big, dirty river comes in from the west and mixes with the clear Mississippi. Where the two waters meet, the Mississippi grows wider and turns brown with mud. The muddy water spreads across the river's surface.

pages.text: The Lower River Another big river comes in from the east. It joins the Mississippi, too. The river grows deep and even wider.
pages.brief: Another big river comes in from the east and joins the Mississippi. The two rivers merge, and the Mississippi grows deeper and even wider than before. The combined water flows on as one broad river.

pages.text: The Mississippi often floods. The floods are messy, but they leave behind rich soil.
pages.brief: The Mississippi floods, and muddy water spreads over the land. The floodwaters cover fields and low ground. The flood looks messy and chaotic, but when the water pulls back, it leaves behind rich soil.

pages.text: The lower part of the river has big cities, too.
pages.brief: The lower part of the river flows past big cities. Tall buildings rise along the wide water, and the river runs through the busy urban landscape. The city sits right beside the lower Mississippi.

pages.text: Boats carry iron, steel, rubber, paper, and wood. Some of these things move back up the river. Some move farther south.
pages.brief: Boats on the river carry iron, steel, rubber, paper, and wood. Some of these materials move back up the river, while others travel farther south toward the sea. The loaded boats move along the wide waterway.

pages.text: River otters play in the upper river. Bald eagles nest in tall trees along the upper river. Pallid sturgeon enter with the Missouri River. Alligators swim in the lower river, where the water is warmer.
pages.brief: A river otter plays in the upper river. A bald eagle nests in a tall tree along the upper river. A pallid sturgeon enters with the Missouri River. An alligator swims in the warmer lower river.

pages.text: The Mighty Mississippi The rain that fell on the lake has reached the sea at last. Some of that water may return to the lake as rain some day. It may make the journey all over again. And again...
pages.brief: The rain that once fell on the lake has reached the sea at last. Some of that water may rise as rain and return to the lake, then make the long journey all over again. The cycle continues again and again.

books.title: What Built This?
books.art_why: The book shows real animals and their structures that exist today, so photographs are possible.

pages.text: Animal Builders Not all builders are human. Some builders are animals! What do they build?
pages.brief: A human builder and a few animal builders are shown outdoors. The animals are busy making their own structures, while the human works nearby. The scene shows that not all builders are human and asks what these animal builders make.

pages.text: Termite Mounds These little insects chew wood. They build huge piles with the wood and mud.
pages.brief: Small termites are shown chewing on pieces of wood. Nearby, a huge mound rises from the ground, built from chewed wood and mud. The little insects work together to make the tall pile.

pages.text: Pufferfish Circles This male fish makes sand art on the floor of the sea. A female fish lays her eggs there.
pages.brief: A male pufferfish is shown on the sandy sea floor, making a circular pattern in the sand. A female pufferfish is nearby, laying her eggs in the sand art he has made.

pages.text: Spider Trapdoors This spider digs a tunnel. It makes a door with its silk. The spider opens the door and prey falls through.
pages.brief: A spider is shown at a tunnel in the ground. It has made a door with its silk. The door is open, and small prey is falling through the opening into the tunnel below.

pages.text: Underground Ant City Millions of ants build underground cities with tunnels that go all over.
pages.brief: Millions of tiny ants are shown underground, moving through tunnels that go all over. Their tunnels spread out in many directions, making an underground city. The ants work together in the big network beneath the ground.

pages.text: Little Ants, Big City.
pages.brief: A large group of tiny ants is shown close together. The ants are very small, but they are part of a big city. The scene focuses on the little ants and the big city they make.

pages.text: Paper Wasp Nests These insects chew bits of wood and plants into paper. They make an amazing nest.
pages.brief: Paper wasps are shown chewing small bits of wood and plants. They turn the bits into paper and use the paper to make an amazing nest. The nest hangs nearby, built from the chewed material.

pages.text: Crayfish Chimneys This animal digs into wet dirt to get to water. The dirt gets pushed up and looks like a little chimney.
pages.brief: A crayfish is shown digging into wet dirt to reach water. As it digs, dirt is pushed up and forms a little mound that looks like a chimney. The crayfish works in the wet ground.

pages.text: Beaver Dams and Dens Beavers use sticks and mud to dams dens build and. Dens are underwater, so beavers have to swim into them. The living space is built above the water level so that it stays dry.
pages.brief: Beavers are shown using sticks and mud to build a dam and a den. The den is underwater, so beavers swim into it. Their living space is above the water level, so it stays dry.

pages.text: Caddisfly Cocoons Watch Them Build Animals don’t need tools to build great things. Animals are amazing!
pages.brief: A caddisfly cocoon is shown in the water, made by a small animal builder. The caddisfly has built its cocoon without tools. The scene shows an animal building a great thing on its own.

books.title: Earth's Water
books.art_why: Real-world water forms and science scenes can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: Water Everywhere Water is in ponds, lakes, and oceans. It flows in rivers and streams. It is in the air and frozen as snow and ice.
pages.brief: A wide natural scene shows a pond, a lake, and an ocean, with a river and a stream flowing through the land. Snow and ice lie on cold ground, and clear air rises above the water and land.

pages.text: Most of Earth is covered with water. Plants and animals need water to live.
pages.brief: Earth is seen from space, mostly blue with water. Below, green plants grow beside a river, and animals gather at the water to drink. The scene shows that plants and animals need water to live.

pages.text: What are some ways you use Earth’s water?
pages.brief: A young child stands beside a broad body of Earth’s water, looking at it with a thoughtful expression. The child’s hands are empty, and the calm scene invites thinking about everyday ways people use water.

pages.text: Different Forms of Water Most of the water we see is a liquid. Liquid water takes the shape of the container it is in.
pages.brief: Clear containers hold liquid water. In one container the water is round and wide; in another it is tall and narrow. The water has taken the shape of each container, showing that liquid water changes shape to match what holds it.

pages.text: Not all water is liquid. When water gets very cold, it freezes. It becomes solid. Solid water is called ice.
pages.brief: A close view shows liquid water turning into solid ice in very cold air. Clear ice pieces sit on a cold surface, with frost around them, showing that when water freezes it becomes a solid.

pages.text: Much of Earth’s frozen water is at the North and South Poles.
pages.brief: At the North Pole and the South Pole, huge stretches of frozen water cover the land and sea. Ice sheets and icy water stretch to the horizon under cold skies, showing much of Earth’s frozen water at the poles.

pages.text: Some of Earth’s water is invisible. It is in the air. This water is a gas.
pages.brief: A clear outdoor view shows open air above land and water, with nothing visible floating in it. The air looks empty, yet this scene represents the invisible water gas that is present in the air.

pages.text: Changing Water Water is always changing. When frozen water is heated, it melts. It changes to a liquid. When liquid water gets cold, it freezes. It changes to ice.
pages.brief: A block of ice sits in a warm spot, with meltwater pooling beside it. Nearby, a small amount of liquid water sits in a cold spot and has begun to freeze into ice, showing water changing between solid and liquid.

pages.text: Have you ever seen a puddle of water dry up on a hot day? Energy from the Sun changed the liquid water into a gas. This is called evaporation.
pages.brief: On a hot, sunny day, a shallow puddle lies on warm ground. The bright Sun shines down, and the puddle is shrinking around its drying edges as its liquid water changes into invisible gas, showing evaporation.

pages.text: When invisible water in the air gets cold, it can make clouds. Clouds are tiny drops of liquid water. Those drops can get bigger. Then they fall as rain.
pages.brief: A wide sky view shows clouds forming in cool air from tiny drops of liquid water that were invisible water gas. Inside the clouds the drops grow bigger and heavier, then fall as rain onto the land below.

pages.text: Water Is Important Rain keeps plants alive. We fight fires with water. Animals take baths in water.
pages.brief: A three-part scene shows rain falling on green plants, helping them stay alive. Firefighters spray water onto a fire. In a river, animals splash and wash themselves in the water, showing important uses of water.

pages.text: It is important to take care of Earth’s water. Polluted water makes people, plants, and animals sick. Would you want to drink and play in polluted water?
pages.brief: Polluted water looks dirty and unsafe. A child stands at the edge, turning away from the water with a worried face. Nearby plants look wilted, and animals look unwell, showing that polluted water can make people, plants, and animals sick.

books.title: Nature Stinks!
books.art_why: Real animals and plants can be photographed today.

pages.text: Stinky Nature Some animals smell bad. Some plants smell bad, too. Being stinky helps some plants and animals stay alive.
pages.brief: Some animals and some plants are shown together. Some animals smell bad, and some plants smell bad too. The bad smell is shown in the scene as part of how these plants and animals stay alive.

pages.text: Stinky Furry Animals This animal sprays a stinky liquid when enemies get close.
pages.brief: A furry animal stands in a natural setting. Enemies get close to it. The animal sprays a stinky liquid at the enemies. The animal faces the enemies as it sprays. The scene focuses on the animal and the close enemies.

pages.text: This animal plays dead if enemies get close. It also makes stinky green slime.
pages.brief: A furry animal is shown with enemies close to it. The animal plays dead by lying still. It also makes stinky green slime. The enemies stay close by as the green slime is shown too.

pages.text: A Very Stinky Plant This animal shoots a stinky liquid at its enemies.
pages.brief: A very stinky plant is shown in the scene. An animal stands facing its enemies and shoots a stinky liquid at them. The liquid comes from the animal toward the enemies. The plant and the animal are both shown.

pages.text: This animal makes stinky liquid to keep other animals away. It also pees on food it doesn’t eat right away. The smell may keep other animals away.
pages.brief: An animal makes stinky liquid to keep other animals away. The animal also pees on food it does not eat right away. The smell may keep other animals away. Other animals are shown nearby. The food is shown with the animal.

pages.text: This animal fights over mates. It uses stinky pee to keep others away.
pages.brief: An animal fights over mates. It uses stinky pee to keep other animals away. The animal and the others are shown together. The fight is over mates, and the stinky pee is part of keeping others away.

pages.text: Stinky Birds This bird eats leaves. Tiny living things in its body break down the leaves. This way of eating makes it smell bad.
pages.brief: A bird eats leaves. Inside the bird’s body, tiny living things break down the leaves. This way of eating makes the bird smell bad. The bird is shown with the leaves it eats. The tiny living things are inside it.

pages.text: This bird eats dead animals. It throws up when enemies get close! Its throw-up smells very bad.
pages.brief: A bird that eats dead animals stands near a dead animal. When enemies get close, the bird throws up. Its throw-up smells very bad. The enemies are close to the bird. The dead animal is on the ground.

pages.text: Stinky Bugs This bug sprays a hot, stinky liquid when enemies get close. The liquid is so hot that it can kill some enemies.
pages.brief: A bug sprays a hot, stinky liquid when enemies get close. The liquid is so hot that it can kill some enemies. The bug and the enemies are shown together. The liquid goes from the bug toward the enemies.

pages.text: This bug is too slow to run away. It makes a stinky liquid when enemies get close.
pages.brief: A bug is too slow to run away. When enemies get close, the bug makes a stinky liquid. The bug and the close enemies are shown together. The stinky liquid is shown with the bug.

pages.text: Other Stinky Animals This turtle is also called “stinkpot”! It smells bad get close. This frog rotten onions get close.
pages.brief: A turtle called a stinkpot is shown. It smells bad when others get close. A frog is shown with rotten onions when others get close. The turtle and the frog are both in the scene.

pages.text: Good and Stinky Some animals smell bad. Some plants smell bad, too. Being stinky helps some plants and animals stay alive.
pages.brief: Some animals are shown with some plants. The animals smell bad, and the plants smell bad too. Being stinky helps these plants and animals stay alive. The bad smell is part of how they stay alive.

books.title: Yellowstone: A Place of Wild Wonders
books.art_why: The keyword check points to drawing; illustrated scenes suit the park's wildlife and history.

pages.text: Introduction National parks are areas of protected land. In 1872, Yellowstone became the first national park. What can people see there?
pages.brief: A wide view of protected Yellowstone land. A small group of people stand in the land and look around at what they can see. The scene presents this land as the first national park in 1872.

pages.text: A Hot Spot People go to Yellowstone to see Old Faithful. Old Faithful is one of the geysers. It shoots steam and hot water high into the air. Yellowstone Supervolcano.
pages.brief: People stand at a distance and watch Old Faithful, a geyser in Yellowstone. A tall column of steam and hot water shoots high into the air from the geyser. The onlookers look up at the eruption.

pages.text: Yellowstone is on top of a hot spot. The hot spot made geysers, hot springs, and hot mud pools.
pages.brief: A view of Yellowstone's ground with geysers, hot springs, and hot mud pools on the surface. Beneath the ground, a hot spot glows under the land. The hot spot is shown feeding the geysers, hot springs, and mud pools above.

pages.text: Wildlife More than 350 kinds of animals live in Yellowstone.
pages.brief: Many different kinds of animals fill a Yellowstone scene. More than 350 kinds of animals are suggested as they stand, walk, and gather across the land. The animals are shown living together in the park.

pages.text: These animals are big and hairy. They roll on the ground to get rid of flies.
pages.brief: Big, hairy animals are shown in Yellowstone. One or more of them roll on the ground, twisting and rubbing their bodies to get rid of flies. The flies are shown near the animals as they roll.

pages.text: These animals are big but fast. They sleep in dens all winter.
pages.brief: Big but fast animals are shown in Yellowstone. In winter, they sleep inside dens. Snow and cold surroundings show the winter season as the animals rest in their dens. The scene shows them settled in the dens for the winter.

pages.text: These animals were forced out of Yellowstone. People brought them back later.
pages.brief: Animals are shown being brought back into Yellowstone by people. The animals had been forced out of the park earlier. People guide the animals into the land, returning them to the park later. The scene shows the return.

pages.text: History Native peoples lived in Yellowstone before it was a national park.
pages.brief: Native peoples are shown living in Yellowstone before it became a national park. They stand, walk, and go about life in the natural landscape. The scene shows their presence in the land before the park was established.

pages.text: More people went to Yellowstone and knew it had to be protected.
pages.brief: More people are shown visiting Yellowstone. They look at the land and understand that it had to be protected. The visitors stand together in the landscape, taking in what they see. Their faces show concern for the place.

pages.text: Today, there are many more national parks.
pages.brief: Many more national parks are shown today. A wide view presents several protected park landscapes, each with natural scenery. People are not needed in every part; the scene simply shows that many more protected places exist today.

pages.text: Conclusion Many people go to Yellowstone every year. They go to fish, hike, and camp in the park.
pages.brief: Many people are shown in Yellowstone during a year. Some fish in the water, some hike along paths, and some camp in the park. The visitors enjoy different activities in the outdoor setting. The scene is busy with visitors.

pages.text: All national parks are great places to see. Yellowstone was the first!
pages.brief: A grand national park landscape is shown as a great place to see. Visitors stand and look out at the natural scenery. Yellowstone is presented as the first national park among all the great parks.

books.title: The Grand Canyon
books.art_why: The Grand Canyon, its river, condors and visitors are real and can be photographed today.

pages.text: A Canyon So Grand The Grand Canyon is so big that it can be seen from space. It became a national park in 1919.
pages.brief: A wide view of the Grand Canyon from high above, showing its enormous size and layered rock walls stretching across the land. The canyon looks vast enough to be seen from space, with open sky above.

pages.text: A national park is an area of protected land. Incredible Condors.
pages.brief: A quiet view of protected canyon land with steep walls and open sky, where several large condors fly or perch. The condors and their habitat are part of a national park, an area of protected land.

pages.text: Formation The Colorado River made the erosion Grand Canyon through. Erosion happens when some of the ground is worn away. The river ran over the earth, and after many years, a canyon was made.
pages.brief: The Colorado River flows over the earth, slowly wearing away the ground over many years. As the river cuts through the land, it carves a deep canyon with steep rocky sides and moving water below.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon is striped with colors. sediment The stripes are layers of that built up on top of each other. They show how Earth has changed over time.
pages.brief: The canyon walls show broad stripes of different colors in the rock. These stripes are layers of sediment that slowly built up on top of each other over time, showing how the Earth has changed.

pages.text: Home in the Grand Canyon Exploration Native people lived in the Grand Canyon. Many still do today.
pages.brief: Native people lived in the Grand Canyon and many still do today. A scene shows Native people sharing daily life in their home area among the canyon rocks, with shelters and community life nearby under open sky.

pages.text: In 1869, a group of Americans went to the canyon. Native people helped them learn about it.
pages.brief: In 1869, a group of American explorers travels through the Grand Canyon. Native people guide them and help them learn about the canyon, pointing out features of the land and the river as they go.

pages.text: The Grand Canyon became a national park. Today, Native people help protect it. A Tale of Two Rims.
pages.brief: Today, the Grand Canyon is a national park with protected land. Native people help protect the park, caring for the land and its natural features while visitors come to see the wide canyon and river.

pages.text: Make Your Own Adventure Many people go to the Grand Canyon every year.
pages.brief: Many people visit the Grand Canyon every year. A large crowd of visitors stands together near the canyon, looking out over the wide landscape and rocky walls under a bright open sky, ready for adventure.

pages.text: Some people hike to the bottom of the canyon. They can walk around the bottom of the canyon for weeks.
pages.brief: Some hikers walk down into the Grand Canyon and reach the bottom. They walk around the canyon floor, where they can keep exploring for long weeks among the rocks, paths, and land below the rim.

pages.text: Some people raft on the Colorado River. The river is very long.
pages.brief: Some people raft on the Colorado River inside the Grand Canyon. The long river carries small rafts through the canyon with wide rocky walls rising on both sides and steady moving water stretching far ahead.

pages.text: Some people walk by the canyon rim. The view from the rim is amazing.
pages.brief: Some people walk along the canyon rim. They look out at the amazing view of the Grand Canyon, with layered rock walls, deep drops, and wide open space stretching far before them under the sky.

pages.text: A Natural Wonder The Grand Canyon will be protected for years to come. People who go there are in for a view like nothing else.
pages.brief: The Grand Canyon is a natural wonder that will be protected for years to come. Visitors stand near the canyon and take in a view like nothing else, with wide layered walls and open sky.

books.title: Hawaii Volcanoes National Park
books.art_why: The book describes a real, present-day national park with active volcanoes, wildlife, and visitors.

pages.text: A Volcano Wonderland Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is on an island in Hawaii. A national park is protected land.
pages.brief: A broad Hawaiian island landscape shows Hawaii Volcanoes National Park as protected land, with a volcano rising above green slopes and the surrounding ocean. The scene is calm and open, with no buildings or people, emphasizing the park’s natural, protected setting.

pages.text: Volcanoes Form a Park A volcano begins with hot, melted rocks deep in the Earth. The rocks push up through the ground. Then the rocks cool. Over time, the rocks build up into volcanoes.
pages.brief: A cutaway view of the ground shows hot, melted rock deep inside the Earth pushing upward through the ground. The rock cools above and builds up in layers, gradually forming a volcano on the surface.

pages.text: Two special volcanoes are in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park.
pages.brief: Two special volcanoes stand in the landscape of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. One rises on the left and one on the right, surrounded by open park land and sky, showing the two volcanoes that the park is known for.

pages.text: One volcano in the park is very active. Leaping Lava.
pages.brief: An active volcano in the park sends bright lava leaping upward and flowing down its side. The scene focuses on the volcano’s hot, moving lava and the rocky ground around it, showing that this volcano is very active.

pages.text: Another volcano in the park is very big.
pages.brief: A very big volcano fills the view in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. Its broad slopes rise high above the surrounding land, with open sky and distant park ground below, making clear how large this second volcano is.

pages.text: An Amazing History Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is 520 square miles (1,347 sq km). People have come to see the volcanoes for a long time.
pages.brief: A wide view of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park shows 520 square miles of protected land with volcanoes in the distance. Visitors stand at a viewpoint, looking out at the volcanoes, showing that people have come to see them for a long time.

pages.text: The land became a national park in 1916.
pages.brief: The land and volcanoes of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park are shown in a wide, old-fashioned view as the area becomes a national park in 1916. Open protected ground and volcanic slopes stretch out under the sky.

pages.text: There are volcanoes and lava tubes. Lava tubes are big tunnels under the ground. People can walk through them.
pages.brief: Inside the park, a lava tube forms a big tunnel under the ground. People walk through the rocky tunnel, moving along its open passage, showing one of the lava tubes that visitors can walk through.

pages.text: Wildlife at the Volcanoes’ Edge Hundreds of animals are protected in the park.
pages.brief: At the volcano’s edge, hundreds of protected animals live in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. A variety of animals gather among rocks and plants, showing the park as a safe place for many kinds of wildlife.

pages.text: Hundreds of plants are protected in the park.
pages.brief: Hundreds of protected plants grow in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. Green plants of different shapes and sizes cover the volcanic ground near the volcanoes, showing the park as a protected place for many kinds of plant life.

pages.text: Enjoy—But Watch Your Step! People can hike or camp in the park.
pages.brief: People hike along a trail and camp in Hawaii Volcanoes National Park. Hikers walk across the volcanic land while campers set up a simple camp nearby, showing ways visitors can enjoy the park while watching their step.

pages.text: When the volcanoes are active, parts of the park close. Hawaii Volcanoes National Park is fun to visit.
pages.brief: When the volcanoes are active, parts of Hawaii Volcanoes National Park close. A closed section near an active volcano is shown, while other visitors enjoy the open park, showing that the park is fun to visit.

books.title: I Collect That!
books.art_why: Collecting real objects and real people exists today, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Introduction Do you own a few stuffed animals? Then you have a collection. A collection is a group of things that are alike.
pages.brief: A young child sits on a bedroom floor beside a low shelf, looking at a group of stuffed animals arranged together. The toys are all alike enough to form one collection, and the child gently touches one of them.

pages.text: People collect things that they like. Some people collect rocks. Other people collect cars.
pages.brief: On one side, a person arranges a group of rocks on a table. On the other side, another person stands beside several cars in a driveway, showing the kinds of things people collect because they like them.

pages.text: Collecting Is Cool A collection can be big or small, such as fifty stamps or ten baseball cards. Some people meet with other people who collect the same things.
pages.brief: A group of collectors meets around a table. Fifty stamps are spread in one area, and ten baseball cards are set in another. The collectors look at the big and small collections together and talk about the items they share.

pages.text: A collection can be hard work. Some people like to care for their collection. They keep count of their things. They keep them clean.
pages.brief: A person carefully cleans collected objects with a soft cloth and counts them one by one at a table. The collection is laid out neatly, and the person keeps every item clean, showing that caring for a collection can take patience and hard work.

pages.text: Common Collections Many people like to collect things that are easy to find. People collect coins and dolls. Math Minute.
pages.brief: A person sorts a pile of coins into small groups and lines up several dolls nearby. These common collections are made from things that are easy to find, and the person looks at them with interest.

pages.text: Some people collect things from places they visit.
pages.brief: A traveler stands in a room with a bag open nearby, placing small objects from a visited place into a collection. The person looks at the gathered items and chooses another one to keep as a reminder of the trip.

pages.text: Other people collect things they find outside.
pages.brief: A child kneels outside in a park or garden, picking up objects found on the ground and placing them into a small container. Leaves, stones, and other outdoor finds form the beginning of a collection.

pages.text: You can also make art out of a collection.
pages.brief: A person sits at a table and arranges collected small objects into a picture, making art from the collection. The objects are sorted by color and shape, and the person places each one carefully to complete the design.

pages.text: What You Collect? Some people collect things based on type. It can take a long time to build a collection. One woman has more than eighteen thousand things with owls. She has owl shirts, owl toys, and more.
pages.brief: A woman stands in a room filled with owl-themed items. She wears an owl shirt and is surrounded by owl toys and many more owl things on shelves, showing a collection built over a long time around one type of object.

pages.text: One man has more than seven hundred locks. Wowser!
pages.brief: A man stands beside shelves and cases filled with more than seven hundred locks. He looks proudly at the large collection, which fills the space around him. The locks are arranged in rows and groups, showing how many he has gathered over time.

pages.text: Start Your Own Collection You can start a collection, too! Why not start with something easy, like fruit stickers? One woman has more than ten thousand!
pages.brief: A woman sits at a table covered with fruit stickers. She places more stickers into albums and onto sheets, sorting them as she goes, showing an easy collection that has grown to more than ten thousand stickers.

pages.text: A collection can also be really strange. Some people collect lists that other people have left behind in food stores! What would you like to collect?
pages.brief: A person stands in a food store aisle holding a stack of paper slips left behind by other shoppers. The slips form an unusual collection, and the person looks at them with curiosity, wondering what to collect next.

books.title: Flies
books.art_why: Flies are real animals living today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: What Are Flies? Flies are insects. There are many kinds of flies.
pages.brief: A close-up group shot of several different kinds of flies resting together on leaves and a stone outdoors in daylight, each fly slightly different in size and shape, showing that there are many kinds of flies and that they are insects.

pages.text: Fly Bodies Flies have one pair of wings. They also have tiny arms that help them steer when they fly.
pages.brief: One fly photographed from above in sharp close-up, its single pair of wings spread wide and the tiny arms near the wings clearly visible as it steers through the air, set against a soft plain background so the wings and body stand out.

pages.text: Flies have eyes that let them see all around. Each eye is made up of many little eyes.
pages.brief: An extreme close-up of a fly's head resting on a leaf, its large eye filling much of the frame, with the many little sections of that eye visible across the shiny surface, showing how the fly sees all around.

pages.text: How Flies Grow and Change All flies start as eggs. Each egg is tiny.
