pages.brief: A tight close-up of a small cluster of fly eggs lying on a damp leaf, each egg a tiny oval, the camera very close so the eggs look small and few, with nothing else in the frame.

pages.text: Out of the egg comes a larva. The larva eats plants, fruits, or dead things. When the larva is grown, it forms a hard cover. It is now a pupa.
pages.brief: A fly larva, a small grub-like young fly, feeding on plant material and a piece of fruit on the ground, with a grown larva beside it forming a hard brown cover around itself as it becomes a pupa.

pages.text: The pupa changes inside the cover. When it comes out, it is an adult. Adult flies do not live very long. Their main job is to lay eggs to make more flies.
pages.brief: An adult fly standing on a leaf beside the hard cover of the pupa it has just come out of, its body fully formed and its wings dry, resting in the open air after the changes inside the cover.

pages.text: How Adult Flies Eat Adult flies drink all their food. They spit on solid food to turn it into goo. Then they drink the goo.
pages.brief: A fly standing on a piece of solid food with its mouthparts down, a small wet patch of goo spreading on the food where it has spat, the fly drinking that goo, photographed very close.

pages.text: Flies and Germs Flies sometimes pick up germs from the things they eat. Some of the germs can make people sick.
pages.brief: A fly walking across food on a surface, its hairy legs and body touching the food, photographed in close-up so the details of its legs are clear as it picks things up while it eats.

pages.text: Some flies suck blood. They can spread germs in the blood from one person to another.
pages.brief: A blood-sucking fly with its mouthparts pressed into a person's skin on an arm, photographed in close-up, with a second person sitting nearby, showing germs passing in the blood from one person to another.

pages.text: Why Flies Are Important Flies spread pollen. Many plants need pollen to make seeds.
pages.brief: A fly covered in yellow pollen dust resting on an open flower in a garden, pollen sticking to its hairy body and legs, with more flowering plants around it in bright daylight.

pages.text: Flies help break down dead plants and animals. Fly eggs and young are food for many other animals.
pages.brief: Flies and their young gathered on a dead plant and a dead animal lying on the ground, breaking the dead things down, while a small bird nearby picks up fly eggs and young as food.

pages.text: Gross but Cool! Flies are amazing insects!
pages.brief: A bright, lively close-up of several flies filling the frame, one caught in mid-air with wings spread and others standing on a leaf, their eyes and wings sharp and detailed in strong daylight.

books.title: Hedgehogs
books.art_why: Hedgehogs are real animals living today, so real photographs suit every page.

pages.text: What Are Hedgehogs? Hedgehogs are mammals. They have sharp quills on their backs.
pages.brief: A single hedgehog stands on short grass in a garden at dusk, its back covered in sharp pointed quills, small dark eyes and a pointed snout visible as it pauses and looks toward the camera.

pages.text: Stay Away! Hedgehogs roll themselves into a ball when they are scared. Their sharp quills stick out to keep other animals away.
pages.brief: A hedgehog has rolled itself into a tight spiky ball on short grass, all its quills sticking out in every direction, its face and legs hidden inside, while a curious dog stands a few steps back on the lawn.

pages.text: Bodies and Senses Hedgehogs have short legs and short tails.
pages.brief: A side view of a hedgehog walking across bare soil, its very short legs close together under the body and its tiny stubby tail showing at the back, quills lying flat along its back.

pages.text: Hedgehogs have eyes, but they do not see well. They can hear and smell very well.
pages.brief: A close view of a hedgehog's face among fallen leaves, its small round eyes open, its wet nose pushed forward as it sniffs the ground, whiskers and soft fur around its snout clearly visible.

pages.text: Why Are They Called That? Hedgehogs look under grass and bushes for food. They also make sounds like little hogs.
pages.brief: A hedgehog pushes its snout under long garden grass and low green bushes, nosing through the stems to search for something to eat, its mouth slightly open and quills raised along its back.

pages.text: What Do They Eat? Hedgehogs eat insects and worms. They also eat spiders, snails, slugs, frogs, toads, lizards, and snakes.
pages.brief: A hedgehog on damp earth beside a worm and a beetle, surrounded by a snail, a slug and a small frog, its snout down close to the ground as it feeds among the insects.

pages.text: Night Animals Hedgehogs do most things at night. They sleep most of the day.
pages.brief: A hedgehog hurries across a moonlit lawn at night, shadows deep and grass silver, while in a second view the same animal sleeps tucked under a pile of dry leaves in daylight.

pages.text: Most hedgehogs roll up in a ball when they sleep.
pages.brief: A hedgehog lies curled tightly into a ball in a nest of dry leaves and grass under a hedge, only the spiky curve of its quills showing, fast asleep in the soft shade.

pages.text: Digging Animals Many hedgehogs live in burrows they dig with their front feet. Hedgehogs sometimes live in burrows dug by hares or foxes.
pages.brief: A hedgehog digs at soft earth with its front feet, half of its body inside a burrow entrance, and nearby a wider burrow opening in the ground sits beneath a tree root.

pages.text: Where Do They Live? Hedgehogs live in Europe, Asia, and Africa. They were brought to New Zealand, and now some live there, too.
pages.brief: Hedgehogs in different settings: one in a European hedgerow, one in an Asian woodland of tall trees, one at the edge of dry African ground, and one in a green New Zealand garden.

pages.text: Leave Me Alone! Hedgehogs live alone for most of their lives. They only live together to have more hedgehogs.
pages.brief: A lone hedgehog walks along a path at night with no other animal near, and in a second view two hedgehogs stand close together nose to nose in the grass.

pages.text: Hedgehogs are funny little animals!
pages.brief: A hedgehog stands upright on its short legs in the grass with its snout lifted, quills catching the light, looking comical and small against a wide, softly blurred green background.

books.title: Our Sun
books.art_why: The Sun, Earth, water, plants, and weather are real subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: What Is the Sun? The Sun is a star. A star is a large ball of gas that gives off energy. The Sun is the closest star to Earth.
pages.brief: The Sun is shown as a huge, glowing star in space: a large ball of gas that gives off energy. Earth appears nearby, clearly showing that this star is the closest star to the Earth.

pages.text: The Sun’s Energy We can feel the Sun’s energy as heat. We can see the Sun’s energy as light. Without heat and light, there would be no life on Earth.
pages.brief: The Sun's energy reaches Earth as heat and light. A person feels the warmth and sees the bright light. Earth is shown as a living world, because heat and light from the Sun are needed for life.

pages.text: Heat from the Sun Without the Sun’s heat, Earth would be too cold. The Sun warms Earth’s land, air, and oceans. Without the Sun’s heat, water would be solid ice.
pages.brief: The Sun shines on Earth, warming the land, air, and oceans. Earth is shown as cold and icy where the Sun's heat is missing, making clear that without heat all water would be solid ice.

pages.text: The Sun’s heat turns ice to liquid water we can drink. All plants and animals need to drink water to live.
pages.brief: The Sun's heat melts ice into liquid water that can be drunk. A plant and an animal are shown with water to drink. The scene makes clear that all plants and animals need to drink water to live.

pages.text: Light from the Sun Without the Sun’s light, Earth would be dark. We need the Sun’s light to see.
pages.brief: The Sun shines light toward Earth. One side of Earth is bright and the other is dark, showing how the Sun's light lets us see. A person looks toward the lit side, because without the Sun's light Earth would be dark.

pages.text: The Sun’s light also helps plants grow. Plants use sunlight to make their own food. Humans and other animals need plants to live.
pages.brief: Sunlight falls on green plants growing in the ground. The plants use sunlight to make their own food. A human and another animal are shown standing nearby, because people and animals need plants to live.

pages.text: The Sun and Weather Without the Sun, there would be no weather. The Sun’s heat turns liquid water to gas.
pages.brief: The Sun shines on liquid water. The Sun's heat turns the liquid water into gas, and the gas is clearly shown rising up from the liquid water. Without the Sun, there would be no weather.

pages.text: The gas rises into the air. When gas in the air gets cold, it turns into clouds.
pages.brief: Gas rises from the water into the air. The gas is shown moving upward. When the gas in the air gets cold, it turns into clouds, and the clouds are shown forming in the sky.

pages.text: Clouds are made of tiny drops of water. When the drops get bigger, they fall as rain, snow, or hail.
pages.brief: Clouds are clearly shown made of tiny drops of water. The tiny drops grow bigger inside the cloud. When the drops are big enough, they then fall from the cloud as rain, snow, or hail.

pages.text: The Sun Is Important Without the Sun’s heat, we would have no water or weather.
pages.brief: The Sun shines above Earth. Its heat is shown as the reason Earth has liquid water and weather. Water and clouds are clearly present, linking the Sun's heat to both water and weather on Earth.

pages.text: Without the Sun’s light, we would have no plants or food. We need the Sun to live on Earth.
pages.brief: Sunlight falls on green plants growing on Earth. The plants are shown as food, and people are shown depending on plants and the Sun. Without the Sun's light, there would be no plants or food.

pages.text: Sun Safety.
pages.brief: A bright Sun shines in the sky. The scene focuses on being safe in the Sun, with the Sun as the central subject. The image stays general, centered on the Sun and the idea of sun safety.

books.title: Ships and Boats
books.art_why: Modern ships, harbours and working boats exist today, so real photographs fit best.

pages.text: Introduction Ships and boats are part of human history. They were once the fastest way to travel.
pages.brief: A wide view of a busy harbour where an old wooden sailing ship and a modern motorboat float side by side on calm blue water, with people on the shore watching the boats come in. The scene shows that ships and boats have carried people through history and were once the quickest way to travel.

pages.text: Early Ships and Boats The first boats were made out of logs. People used poles to push the boats.
pages.brief: Two people stand in a shallow river beside a thick, stripped log floating on the water. Each holds a long wooden pole pushed down into the riverbed to move the log boat forward, and ripples spread around the log. Green banks and reeds line the water behind them.

pages.text: Other boats used paddles or oars. The oars pushed against the water to move the boats.
pages.brief: A wooden boat glides across open water with two people aboard, each gripping a long wooden oar. The oar blades press into the water and push it back in a splash of white, driving the boat forward, while the rowers lean into the stroke under a clear sky.

pages.text: Later, people made boats with wooden frames. They covered the frames with bark or animal skins.
pages.brief: On a grassy shore, people bend over a wooden frame of thin branches, stretching animal skins and sheets of bark over it and tying them down. A finished skin-covered boat sits nearby on the water, ready to float, with trees and a riverbank behind.

pages.text: Frame boats were larger than log boats. Many people could row at the same time.
pages.brief: A large wooden frame boat floats on a wide river with many people sitting along both sides, each holding an oar. They row together in time, the long boat moving steadily forward while others on the bank watch the bigger boat pass by.

pages.text: Sails were used to move boats, too. The sails caught the wind to push the boat.
pages.brief: A small boat with a single cloth sail moves across rippling blue water. The sail billows out, filled by the wind, and pushes the boat forward while a person at the back steers. Open water stretches to the horizon and clouds drift above.

pages.text: Larger ships needed more sails. Sailing ships carried people around the world.
pages.brief: A tall sailing ship with several masts and many large sails crosses the open sea, its sails full of wind. Sailors work on the deck and in the rigging, and the ship leans slightly as it carries people on a long voyage around the world.

pages.text: Modern Ships and Boats Many ships and boats today are made of metal or plastic. They often use engines to move through the water.
pages.brief: A modern boat made of smooth metal and a smaller plastic boat float at a dock. Below the deck an engine hums and churns the water behind the boat into white foam as it moves through the harbour past other moored boats and wooden posts.

pages.text: Some boats do special jobs. Tugboats push and pull larger ships. Ferryboats carry cars and people. Fireboats put out fires on other ships.
pages.brief: Three working boats are shown: a sturdy tugboat nudging a huge ship in a harbour, a ferryboat loaded with cars and passengers crossing to a dock, and a red fireboat spraying a tall stream of water toward a smoking ship. Harbour buildings stand behind them.

pages.text: Many countries use ships and boats to help defend them.
pages.brief: Ships of a country's navy sail in formation across grey water, with sailors in uniform standing on deck. Flags fly from the mast of the lead ship while the boats patrol together, guarding the coast, with a low shoreline visible in the distance.

pages.text: People still use smaller boats for fishing and fun. Many small boats still use paddles or oars.
pages.brief: Two small boats rest on a quiet lake in golden evening light. In one, a person holds a fishing rod; in the other, a family laughs and paddles with wooden oars, water dripping from the blades. Trees and a small wooden jetty line the shore behind them.

pages.text: Conclusion Ships and boats are still an important part of our world.
pages.brief: A wide harbour scene at sunset shows old and new boats together, a wooden rowing boat, a sailing ship and a modern motor vessel, all floating on the same blue water while people on the quay look out, showing that ships and boats are still important in our world.

books.title: Spring Is Here
books.art_why: Spring plants, animals, weather and places exist today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: The Warmer Days of Spring Remember how the sun feels on the first warm day of spring? In spring, each day grows longer and warmer.
pages.brief: A bright spring sun shines in a clear sky above open ground. Warm sunlight spreads across the scene on the first warm day of spring. The view shows only the sun and the warmer, longer day, with no people or animals added.

pages.text: The plants and animals feel it grow warmer, too.
pages.brief: Green plants and small animals sit outdoors in the warming air. Leaves and stems stand in the soft light while tiny creatures feel the growing warmth around them. The scene shows plants and animals together as spring warmth reaches the ground.

pages.text: The Garden The flowers send up shoots from round white bulbs. Soon the garden will be filled with color.
pages.brief: In a garden, round white bulbs sit in dark soil. Green shoots push up from the bulbs toward the light. The garden bed is bare around them, ready soon to be filled with color from the growing flowers.

pages.text: The robins are back at work. They collect brown grass for a nest. Soon they will feed wiggly worms to hungry babies.
pages.brief: Two robins work in a garden, gathering brown grass for a nest. One robin holds dry grass in its beak while the other stands nearby. Their nest rests among the branches, ready for the babies they will soon feed wiggly worms.

pages.text: The Woods The trees are growing again. The fat buds on a tree grow into big, flat leaves. Caterpillars nibble on them.
pages.brief: In the woods, trees grow again. Fat buds on a tree open into big, flat leaves. A caterpillar nibbles on a green leaf beside the buds and branches. The woodland is filling with new leaves and hungry caterpillars.

pages.text: The cricket comes out from underground. It rubs its wings to make the sound “chirp, chirp.”
pages.brief: A cricket comes out from underground, climbing into the open air. It rubs its wings together to make a chirping sound. The small insect sits near the soil opening, with its wings raised as it chirps in the spring air.

pages.text: The Mountains In the mountains, snow melts away. Streams fill with water.
pages.brief: In the mountains, snow melts away. Water runs down the slopes and fills streams. The mountain scene shows patches of melting snow and clear water rushing along the ground, turning into streams that carry the spring melt through the rocky landscape.

pages.text: The bear comes out from her underground den. She is hungry.
pages.brief: A bear comes out from her underground den. She steps into the open air, looking hungry after her long rest. The bear stands near the den opening, with the ground around her as spring arrives in the mountain area.

pages.text: The Meadow A baby deer drinks its mother’s milk. Soon it will eat soft spring grass.
pages.brief: In a meadow, a baby deer drinks milk from its mother. The mother deer stands close while the fawn nurses. Soft spring grass grows around them, and soon the baby deer will eat the grass instead of milk.

pages.text: Gophers kick up piles of brown soil. They nibble on dandelion leaves.
pages.brief: Gophers kick up piles of brown soil in the meadow. One gopher nibbles on dandelion leaves while another pushes soil into a small mound. The meadow floor shows loose brown earth and green dandelion leaves around the busy gophers.

pages.text: The Pond It’s also warmer at the pond. The turtles lie on a log in the sun.
pages.brief: At the pond, the water is warmer. Turtles lie on a log in the sun. Their shells rest along the wood as they soak up the spring warmth. The pond water surrounds the log, and the turtles stay still in the bright sunlight.

pages.text: A water lily ’s flat, round leaf lies on top of the water. A frog sits on the leaf and makes a sound, “ribbet, ribbet.” Spring is here.
pages.brief: A water lily’s flat, round leaf floats on top of the pond water. A frog sits on the leaf, making a ribbet sound. The frog rests on the green leaf, and the pond shows spring is here.
